conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for taking the time to meet with me. I’m Dr. Walker, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here simply to check in on how things have been feeling for you since your baby arrived. We’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s just ten questions that help us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up in the first year postpartum, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can keep you safe and supported.  

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team. There are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. We’ll go one question at a own pace; you can pause, clarify, or take breaks anytime. Ready to start?  

First, thinking back over the **past seven days**, have you been able to **laugh and see the funny side of things**?

[pauses, eyes a bit teary]  
I… I can still laugh sometimes—like when my little one makes those silly milk-drunk faces—but it feels forced. Most of the time I just don’t find things funny the way I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I’ll smile if my partner shows me a cute video, but it’s like the laughter fades right away. Things that used to crack me up just feel kind of flat now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[sighs softly]  
A few things, I guess—like when my mom offers to take the baby for a walk, I do look forward to that little break—but mostly I don’t feel that bubbly excitement I used to get. Even coffee with a friend feels more like something I “should” do than something I truly want.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” Yesterday I couldn’t settle her for an hour and I kept thinking, “A good mom would know what she needs.” I know, logically, babies just cry, but the guilt still hits.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[twists the edge of her sleeve]  
Almost every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly picture her blanket sliding over her face or her choking on spit-up, even though I know she’s fine. My heart races and it’s hard to shut the thoughts off… sometimes it takes me a while to breathe normally again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[eyes widen a little]  
Yeah… a couple of times this week. Once, I was just folding laundry while she napped and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe—my chest got tight and I thought something horrible was about to happen. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky. I didn’t have any real reason to feel that way.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a slow breath]  
Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, and I’m staring at it all thinking, “How can I not handle this?” I still get through it, but it’s like walking through quicksand.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]  
Yeah… I lie down after the last feed and my head just keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she breathing, am I cut out for this? It takes me maybe an hour to drift off, then I jolt awake at every little sound. I end up getting maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

[sighs, eyes glassy]  
Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a gray cloud hanging over me. I’ll be rocking her and tears just start rolling—no real trigger. The sadness feels heavy, and even when I tell myself I should be happy, it doesn’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[ voice cracks a little ]  
Yeah… it’s happened twice in the past week. Once was at 3 a.m. when she wouldn’t latch; I just sat there in the nursery with tears streaming, feeling like I’d failed her. The other time was after a phone call with my mom—she asked how I was doing and I couldn’t hold it in.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[pauses, looks down]  
…A couple of times. Nothing planned—I’d never leave her—but when everything feels too heavy, the thought flashes: “What if I just wasn’t here?” It scares me, and I push it away, but it’s shown up once or twice this week.

You've shared that since your baby arrived you feel as though a gray cloud is following you most days-laughter fades quickly, excitement is replaced by obligation, and simple tasks feel like walking through quicksand. You tear up without warning, blame yourself whenever your baby fusses, lie awake running through frightening "what-ifs," and have even had brief, scary thoughts of escape. At the same time you love your daughter fiercely and want to be the best mum you can be; this tension between devotion and despair is exhausting.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges only brief, weak amusement and describes loss of lasting laughter, aligning with "definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only limited enjoyment in a few situations and explicitly states "I don't feel that bubbly excitement I used to get," aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring "pretty often" and gives a recent example, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive, uncontrollable anxious thoughts almost daily with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient described sudden unexpected panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, fear of impending doom) occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and impaired coping most days, matching "sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing thoughts, resulting in only four broken hours of sleep—clearly "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive sadness daily with uncontrollable tears and persistent heaviness, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports two crying episodes in the past week triggered by infant-feeding struggles and maternal concern, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive self-harm thoughts occurring "a couple of times" and "once or twice this week," matching the "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 on the EPDS places you well above the ≥14 threshold that signals probable major depression and mandates urgent evaluation. You endorsed frequent or severe symptoms on nine of ten items, including <sym>loss of enjoyment</sym>, <sym>near-daily crying</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic spells</sym>, <sym>overwhelm</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, and <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym>. These findings align closely with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Because item 10 scored ≥1, immediate safety assessment is required. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline, both compatible with breastfeeding
3. Enlist trusted family or friends to help with overnight infant care so you can obtain 4- to 5-hour blocks of sleep
4. Call the national maternal mental-health helpline (24/7, 1-833-943-5746) or text "HELLO" to 741741 if distress escalates or self-harm thoughts return
5. Remove or secure potentially harmful items and create a written safety plan tonight; bring it to your appointment
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress once treatment begins
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression Screen  
Date: [today’s date]  
Clinician: [name], LCSW

Identified Symptoms / Emotional Concerns:
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Daily, intrusive anxiety and catastrophic worry about infant safety (Q4)  
- Two discrete panic episodes without clear trigger (Q5)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and unable to cope with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent insomnia (Q7)  
- Passive suicidal ideation (“What if I just wasn’t here?”) without plan or intent, occurring twice this week (Q10)

Pattern Summary:
Patient reports a two-week (or longer) cluster of depressive symptoms, functional impairment, and comorbid anxiety consistent with possible peripartum mood/anxiety disorder. Passive SI present; no protective-plan expressed.

Risk Flags:
- Active suicidal ideation (passive)  
- Significant anhedonia and hopelessness  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination  
- High maternal self-criticism and guilt  

Screening Impression:
High clinical concern for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and co-occurring anxiety; safety risk elevated due to presence of suicidal thoughts. Recommend immediate formal evaluation (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and safety planning; consider expedited referral to perinatal psychiatry or crisis service as clinically indicated.

No diagnosis rendered; screening only.
